newsitem.title: USA: Judge dismisses part of Miami airport bond lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Judge dismisses part of Miami airport bond lawsuit.

text.p: A federal judge dismissed part of the lawsuit filed by five airlines seeking to block bond financing of the new American Airlines terminal at Miami International Airport, attorneys in the case said on Friday.

U.S. District Judge Joan Lenard put the remaining complaints in the suit on hold on Thursday pending a review by the Federal Aviation Authority. The lawsuit had been set to go to trial on November 12.

The airlines sued Dade County, which runs the airport, seeking to block the revenue bond financing plan. The carriers, who also fly out of Miami International, said their rents would have to be raised to pay debt service on the bonds for a $975 million facility that only American could use.
The plaintiffs are Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Trans World Airlines Inc, USAir Group Inc and United Airlines, a unit of UAL Corp.

Lawyers for the county and American said the American terminal was part of a 10-year, $3.6 billion expansion that would include another new terminal for the other carriers, plus a new runway and added cargo space.

They said American would help pay for the other carriers' facilities and the funding formula, which is pro rated according to the number of flights each carrier operates, has long been the norm at Miami and other airports.
Alvin Davis, attorney for American, said Lenard dismissed the plaintiffs' claim that the revenue increase needed to pay debt service amounted to an illegal head tax on passengers.
She also dismissed Air Canada's contention that the funding proposal would violate a commerce treaty between the United States and Canada.
Lenard asked the FAA to determine whether or not the airport fee structure is fair and reasonable.
"That is an issue that the FAA deals with routinely and customarily," Davis said.

A ruling is expected within six months. Lenard would then address one final claim, that contracts between the airport and the carriers gives some of the larger airlines a "majority in interest" right to veto airport construction projects.

The bulk of the bonds for the project have not yet been issued, although $25 million from a $292 million issue in February was earmarked for eningeering and design work on the American terminal. That work is still in the preliminary stages.
"This really shouldn't slow anything up at all," Davis said of the lawsuit.
